title: Reading wave diagrams and graphs
keyIdea: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant, so the gap from crest to crest along it is the wavelength. A displacement–time graph follows one point as time passes, so the crest-to-crest gap is the period. On both, the amplitude is measured from the rest line up to a crest.

kid: Wave graphs often look the same, so always read the label on the bottom axis first. It tells you what the graph shows.
If the bottom axis says distance, the graph is like a photo of the whole wave at one moment. Crest to crest along it gives the wavelength, in metres.
If the bottom axis says time, the graph follows one spot, like a buoy, as it bobs up and down. Crest to crest gives the period: the time for one bob, in seconds.
The side axis shows how far a spot is from where it rests. Measure from the middle line up to a crest. That is the amplitude. Top to bottom is twice as big.
adult: Both graphs plot displacement, the distance of a point from its rest position, on the vertical axis. The horizontal axis decides the meaning. Against distance, the curve is the shape of the medium at one instant, and one repeat of the pattern is the wavelength λ. Against time, the curve is the history of a single point, and one repeat is the period T.

Amplitude is the maximum displacement, read from the zero line to a crest (or to a trough). Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T, so a period of 0.5 s means 2 Hz. Combining the two graphs gives the speed: v = λ/T = fλ.

To read a repeat accurately, measure across several waves and divide: if 3 whole waves span 4.5 m, λ = 1.5 m. Any two matching points work, such as two crests, two troughs, or two zeros where the curve rises.

Common mistakes: taking crest to trough as the amplitude (it is twice the amplitude), taking crest to the next trough as a whole wavelength (it is half), calling the gap on a time graph a wavelength, and writing the period where the frequency is asked for. Checking the axis label and the unit catches most of these.

familyTip: Draw a wavy line on paper and label the bottom axis "distance (m)". Ask: what is crest to crest? Then relabel it "time (s)" and ask again. The drawing is the same, but the answer changes from a wavelength to a period.

worked.title: Reading a displacement–time graph
steps: The bottom axis says time (s), so this graph follows one point and gives the period, not the wavelength.
Crests are at 0.2 s, 1.0 s and 1.8 s. Two crests span 1.8 − 0.2 = 1.6 s for 2 waves, so T = 0.8 s.
The crests reach 3 cm and the troughs −3 cm, so the amplitude is 3 cm, not 6 cm.

practice.prompt: A wave graph has "time (s)" on its horizontal axis. The gap from one crest to the next is…
practice.hint: Look at the unit of the horizontal axis. A gap along it is measured in that unit.
practice.explain: The gap is a time, in seconds, so it is the period: the time for one full oscillation. A wavelength would be a distance, read off a distance axis.

practice.prompt: On a displacement–distance graph, one crest is at {a} m and the next crest is at {=a+b} m. What is the wavelength, in metres?
practice.hint: One wavelength is the gap between two neighbouring crests. Subtract the two positions.

practice.prompt: A wave's crests reach {a} cm above the rest line and its troughs reach {a} cm below. What is the amplitude, in cm?
practice.hint: Amplitude is measured from the rest line, not from the bottom of a trough.
practice.explain: The amplitude is the biggest displacement from the rest line: {a} cm. Crest to trough is {=2*a} cm, which is twice the amplitude.

practice.prompt: On a displacement–distance graph, a crest is at 1.0 m and the next trough is at 1.5 m. What is the wavelength?
practice.hint: Crest to the next trough is only part of a wave. How much of one?
practice.explain: Crest to the next trough is half a wave, 0.5 m, so a whole wavelength is 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 m.

practice.prompt: On a displacement–time graph, the crests are at {a} s, {=a+b} s and {=a+2*b} s. What is the period, in seconds?
practice.hint: The period is the time from one crest to the next on a time graph.
practice.explain: Each crest comes {b} s after the one before, so the period is {b} s.

pool.prompt: Two wave graphs look exactly alike. One has "distance (m)" on its horizontal axis and the other has "time (s)". What does the crest-to-crest gap show on each?
choices: Wavelength on the distance graph, period on the time graph
Period on the distance graph, wavelength on the time graph
pool.hint: A gap along an axis is measured in that axis's unit. Which quantity is a length, and which is a time?
pool.explain: A gap in metres along the distance axis is a wavelength; a gap in seconds along the time axis is a period. Same shape, different meaning.

pool.prompt: A buoy bobs up and down {a} times in 10 seconds. What is the frequency, in Hz?
pool.hint: Frequency is the number of oscillations in one second. Divide the count by the time.

pool.prompt: On a displacement–distance graph, a crest is {a} m from the next trough. What is the wavelength, in metres?
pool.hint: Crest to the next trough covers half of one whole wave.
pool.explain: Crest to trough is half a wavelength, so the wavelength is 2 × {a} = {=2*a} m.

pool.prompt: A displacement–time graph shows crests 0.25 s apart. What is the frequency?
pool.hint: The gap is the period. How many periods of 0.25 s fit in 1 s?
pool.explain: The period is 0.25 s, so f = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 Hz: four waves pass each second. 0.25 is the period, not the frequency.

pool.prompt: A displacement–distance graph shows {a} whole waves across 12 m. What is the wavelength, in metres?
pool.hint: Divide the total distance by the number of whole waves it holds.
pool.explain: 12 m ÷ {a} waves = {=12/a} m per wave, so λ = {=12/a} m.

pool.prompt: On a displacement–time graph the curve goes from +5 cm at a crest down to −5 cm at a trough. Which statement is right?
choices: The amplitude is 0 cm, because +5 and −5 cancel
pool.hint: Measure from the zero line, where the point rests, to the top of a crest.
pool.explain: The amplitude is the largest displacement from rest, 5 cm. Crest to trough, 10 cm, is twice the amplitude.

pool.prompt: What does the vertical axis show on both a displacement–distance and a displacement–time graph of a wave?
choices: How far a point is from its rest position
How far the wave has travelled
The time since the wave started
pool.hint: Both graphs are named "displacement – something". Which word belongs to the vertical axis?
pool.explain: Displacement goes up the side on both graphs: how far a point is above or below where it rests. Only the horizontal axis changes, distance or time.

pool.prompt: A wave has wavelength 2 m (from its distance graph) and period 0.5 s (from its time graph). What is its speed?
pool.hint: Speed = wavelength ÷ period, because the wave moves one wavelength in each period.
pool.explain: v = λ ÷ T = 2 m ÷ 0.5 s = 4 m/s. Multiplying 2 × 0.5 = 1 would treat the period as if it were the frequency.

pool.prompt: On a displacement–time graph, the crests are 2 s apart. Someone writes "wavelength = 2 m". What went wrong?
choices: A time graph gives the period, 2 s, not the wavelength
Nothing: the gap is the wavelength
The wavelength should be half, 1 m
pool.hint: Check the unit on the horizontal axis before naming the gap.
pool.explain: The horizontal axis is time, so the gap is 2 s, the period. You cannot get a wavelength from a time graph alone; you need a distance graph or the speed.

visual.caption: Change the amplitude and frequency until your wave matches the faint target, then read both values off the graph.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: one wave, two graphs. Measure crest to crest across distance, then across time, and see which gap is the wavelength and which is the period.
